body_en:
*The Niner Empire Germany e.V. · Draft analysis by Chris Pracher*

## Is John Lynch really such a bad drafter, or just one of many?

A data-driven analysis based on wAV statistics (Pro-Football-Reference, 2017–2025)

May 2026 · 2,312 picks · 32 teams · 9 draft classes

## Introduction: the narrative and the numbers

By now it is a fixture of the 49ers discourse: John Lynch can't draft. Every failed first-round pick becomes a lament, every below-average pick an indictment. The discussion, both in the US, where [Warren Sharp](https://x.com/SharpFootball/status/2048232349536555359) wrote a long piece on John Lynch's drafts, and in German-language podcasts such as Fokus Football, where analyst Valentin Rödiger was harsh on Lynch, is usually emotional and rarely backed by concrete numbers in their overall context. This analysis aims to change that.

For this analysis, all 2,312 NFL draft picks from 2017 to 2025 were evaluated: all 32 teams, all seven rounds. The basis is Pro-Football-Reference's weighted Approximate Value (wAV), one of the few objective career-value metrics in American football, supplemented by a quantitative measure of long-term league tenure (active roster data). The result: over the full period, the San Francisco 49ers rank 7th of 32 teams in wAV and even 2nd in the number of players still active in the NFL, the top quarter of the league. With clearly measurable strengths, identifiable weaknesses and a more recent weak phase that can be explained structurally.

## Methodology: wAV and wAVOE

Before getting into the numbers, it is necessary to explain what the following sections measure with, and why this metric is well suited to the question but also has clear limits.

**Weighted Approximate Value (wAV): what is it?**

Weighted Approximate Value (wAV) is a metric developed by Doug Drinen at Pro-Football-Reference that tries to express an NFL player's career value in a single number, independent of position and across many seasons. That sounds easier than it is: how do you compare the value of a dominant left guard with that of a Pro Bowl cornerback? How do you rate an injury-prone star against a solid, long-time starter?

The concept behind it is the Approximate Value (AV) per season, from which wAV is calculated. The calculation follows a two-step approach:

- **Season AV:** Pro-Football-Reference calculates an annual value contribution for each player based on starts, snaps, Pro Bowl selections, All-Pro teams and position-specific performance indicators (e.g. sacks for edge rushers, receiving yards for wide receivers, blocks for offensive linemen). The value ranges roughly from 0 (no meaningful contribution) to more than 19 (elite season, All-Pro level).
- **Career weighting:** wAV is not simply the sum of all seasons: it weights the best season at 100%, the second-best at 95%, the third-best at 90% and so on. That makes sense: a player who had one elite season and then declined is more valuable than someone who played ten middling seasons.

**Worked example: Nick Bosa (SFO, R1 2019, pick #2)**

Season AV values (simplified): 2019: 15 • 2021: 19 • 2022: 19 • 2023: 12 • 2024: 9

wAV weighting: 19 × 1.0 + 19 × 0.95 + 15 × 0.90 + 12 × 0.85 + 9 × 0.80 = approx. 58

A player with AV values of 5, 5, 5, 5, 5 would only reach a wAV of ≈22, even though he has the same season total as someone with 10, 7, 5, 0, 3 (wAV ≈18). Peak seasons count more.

**What wAV measures, and what it doesn't**

wAV measures career impact, not draft value for a particular team. That is an important distinction: if the 49ers draft a player who later blossoms on another team, it still counts positively toward the Niners' wAV. This is deliberate: the point is to judge whether a team recognizes good players, not whether it uses them optimally. The latter is coaching, not scouting.

What wAV measures well:

- Long-term starter quality (several strong seasons)
- Position-independent career value
- Whether a pick had "franchise impact"

What wAV doesn't measure:

- Scheme fit: a player who never shows his potential in the wrong system gets less wAV than he would have deserved
- Snap counts vs. quality: a starter with 1,000 middling snaps can get more wAV than a backup with 300 elite snaps
- Special teams (only partially included)

**Methodology conclusion:** wAV is probably the best freely available, public metric for long-term player value in the NFL draft. It isn't perfect, but it is better than any alternative. Proxies often used by the media, such as Pro Bowl selections or starts in year 2, are even more prone to noise.

**wAV over expected (wAVOE): the heart of the analysis**

The biggest weakness of raw wAV in the draft context is time bias: a player from 2017 had eight years to accumulate wAV. A 2025 rookie has had just one season. That is why wAVOE (wAV over expected) comes in: the difference between a player's actual wAV and the expected value of his slot. This expected value is calculated as the empirical average of all other picks in the same round in the same draft year.

That way, wAVOE automatically solves the timing problem: the expected value of R2/2020 picks already includes the fact that these players had five years. An R2/2025 pick only competes with other R2/2025 picks.

**Worked example wAVOE: Deebo Samuel**

Deebo Samuel (SFO, R2 #36, 2019): wAV = 52

Average of all R2 picks in 2019: approx. 22.3

wAVOE Deebo Samuel = +29.7

A fictional player with the identical wAV of 52 but drafted in R4 would have a wAVOE of +34, because the expectation for his slot was lower. The slot context counts.

**Definition of hit / bust in this analysis:**

Instead of relying on the relative wAVOE comparison within a round, which would lead to similar rates across all rounds, an absolute standard based on wAV per season is applied for the hit/bust rate: hit = ≥ 5 wAV per season, i.e. the player consistently produces at a solid starter level. Bust = < 1.5 wAV per season with at least two seasons of experience, rounds 1–4 only (in the late rounds there are no "busts," since there is no starter expectation). As a result, the rates differ significantly between rounds: in round 1, 57% of all picks become hits, in round 7 only 2.6%. That matches football reality.

## How hard drafting really is

Before the 49ers are evaluated, the context has to be set. The actual hit rates across all 2,312 picks of the last nine years are sobering:

| Round | Picks | Avg. wAV | Hit rate* | Bust rate** | Assessment |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| R1 (1–32) | 287 | 27.1 | 57.1% | 7.3% | Just over every 2nd becomes a starter |
| R2 (33–64) | 288 | 17.8 | 32.3% | 21.2% | Only every 3rd reaches starter level |
| R3 (65–105) | 354 | 13.4 | 16.9% | 33.1% | Every 3rd is a bust |
| R4 (106–140) | 331 | 9.1 | 7.6% | 45.6% | Hardly any hits, many busts |
| R5 (141–175) | 342 | 7.5 | 6.1% | – | Rarely starter level |
| R6 (176–215) | 364 | 5.0 | 1.9% | – | Almost never a hit |
| R7 (216+) | 346 | 3.5 | 2.6% | – | Purdy is the exception |

Table 1: League-wide hit and bust rates by round, 2017–2025 (n = 2,312). *Hit = ≥ 5 wAV per season. **Bust = < 1.5 wAV per season with ≥ 2 years, R1–R4 only.

What these numbers show: even in round 1, where talent and scouting effort are highest, only just over every second pick reaches lasting starter level. From round 3 on, the hit rate drops below 17%. In round 4, almost half of all picks are busts. The early rounds are no guarantee of quality; they only shift the probability.

The bust rate is particularly interesting: in round 1 it is surprisingly low at 7.3%, because even weaker first-round picks are often on the field enough thanks to physical superiority to accumulate wAV. From round 3 on, the bust rate explodes to over 33%: this is where players disappear from every NFL roster after two years.

What stands out in the overall table: the top teams are not simply the teams with the most Super Bowls in this period. *Phase 1: 2017–2021 · rebuild · rank 5 of 32*

## Phase 1 (2017–2021): Lynch as an elite drafter

The first five years under Lynch and Shanahan are among the most remarkable rebuild phases in recent NFL history. For this period, the 49ers rank 5th of 32 with an average wAVOE of +3.25, and that despite three historically bad first-round picks. It's hard to imagine what would have happened had they taken Patrick Mahomes instead of Solomon Thomas in 2017, or had they not needlessly beaten the Rams in the second-to-last game of 2016 and thereby had a shot at Myles Garrett with the No. 1 pick.

What distinguishes this period is the completely above-average day-3 rate: Kittle, DJ Jones, Hufanga, Greenlaw, Reed (who never really played for the 49ers, though): five starter-quality players from the last three rounds for a single franchise.

The R1 record is the mirror image: together, Foster, Thomas and Lance wipe out more than 76 points of negative wAVOE in just three picks. And it is still enough for rank 5, proof of how dominant the remaining picks were.

**Why Shanahan teams master the late rounds**

The outstanding day-3 record is no coincidence. Shanahan's system has specific but learnable requirements: outside zone runners need certain athletic profiles, receivers need route precision and timing more than raw speed, tight ends have to be able to block and catch. This precision in the requirements allows the scouting department to identify players in later rounds who are built exactly for this system, even if their general NFL athleticism isn't worthy of day 1 or day 2.

George Kittle was drafted late partly because other teams didn't need his blocking skills as an inline TE, which are central to Shanahan's run-heavy offense and have since been copied by half the league (in addition to the fact that he was often injured in college and didn't have the best reputation). Fred Warner had been a safety at BYU, but because of his football intelligence Robert Saleh and DeMeco Ryans saw him as a Mike linebacker. Dre Greenlaw was too slow for many scouting boards, but ideally suited for defenses that play two-gap principles. That is the core of the approach: not the best available player for the league, but the right player for this system.

**Context, Trey Lance:** The Lance pick didn't just cost the Niners 22.3 wAVOE; it also cost them their 2022 and 2023 first-round picks. That is the structurally most important legacy shaping the next phase. For comparison: the Buffalo Bills had two first-round picks each in 2022 and 2023. This difference in pick inventory explains a considerable part of the performance gap between the two teams in this period.

*Phase 2: 2022–2025 · competitive window · rank 16 of 32*

## Phase 2 (2022–2025): collapse or context?

At first glance, the current phase looks like a drop in quality: average wAVOE −0.15, rank 16/32, league average. Behind it are two structural explanations.

**Structural problem 1: a general lack of premium picks**

Because of the Lance trade (2021) and the CMC trade (2022), the Niners had only two first-round picks among their 37 picks in this phase (#31 Pearsall 2024, #11 Williams 2025), compared with a league average of about four per team.

**Structural problem 2: deliberate roster optimization instead of best player available**

In 2022 and 2023, the 49ers were a highly competitive team: twice in the NFC Championship Game, one Super Bowl appearance. With a well-established, highly paid roster, there was hardly any room for development players.

Lynch and Shanahan therefore deliberately adopted a different draft philosophy: targeted filling of roster gaps instead of consistent best player available or high-ceiling players. Danny Gray was supposed to fill the gap of a speedy deep WR, Tyrion Davis-Price was to serve as a physical runner, Jake Moody was to save cap space as a cost-efficient kicker. These picks weren't pure evaluation mistakes but situational decisions, and they communicated it openly at the time:

**Shanahan and Lynch in their own words (2022/2023):**

**"Best available role, not best available player":** In their post-draft press conferences in 2022 and 2023, Lynch and Shanahan explicitly emphasized that they only make picks when the player can take on a clearly defined role in the system: rotation, special teams, depth or as a future starter. No pick without a realistic chance of making the roster.

**The veteran argument:** Especially at positions with strong veterans, both said explicitly that they don't bring in anyone on talent alone if he has hardly any realistic chance of displacing the established players; otherwise "you waste the pick."

**Goal: every pick should make the 53-man roster.** Shanahan emphasized that with every pick, they hoped the player would stick on the roster. That's why for later picks they often chose day-1 contributors with a clear role (special teams, third DE, backup safety) instead of pure development rookies who would very likely not have gotten a roster spot because of strong veterans.

In one sentence: Lynch and Shanahan steered their 2022/2023 drafts toward getting players who would realistically get a role and stick on the roster, instead of picking talents who would very likely not have gotten a roster spot because of strong veterans and would have been cut.

That this strategy was wrong in hindsight is obvious, and Lynch and Shanahan have since admitted it themselves. The short-term roster logic came at the expense of long-term draft quality. On top of that, the Lance trade continues to weigh heavily.

What the table also shows: 2022–2025 is a difficult evaluation period for many teams. Bust rates are falling league-wide because many picks simply haven't had enough time to get their careers going. The phase 2 numbers will read differently in three years.

**A signal for the future:** of the 19 players in the 2024 and 2025 classes, 18 are still on the roster, a clear sign that the philosophy has changed. Away from situational roster management, toward consistent talent scouting.

**Pearsall and Williams, judged too early:** both have negative wAVOE values after one and two seasons respectively, which is the rule for first-round rookies, not the exception. Deebo Samuel had hardly any numbers after year 1; today he stands at a wAVOE of +29.9. Nick Bosa was at +8 OE after year 1 and at +20.7 after nine years.

- **Round 1, a systematic weakness in every period (−6.47 / −7.38 / −3.25 OE):** three different eras, the same tendency. First-round evaluation is the Achilles' heel.
- **Round 5, absolute league-best strength in the rebuild phase (+16.36 OE):** weakened in the competitive window (−1.44) by fewer picks and a lack of late-round resources.

A revealing detail: round 7 is the only round in which the Niners stay positive across all three periods. That reflects a peculiarity of the Shanahan system: very late picks can have a disproportionately large impact in this scheme if they have the right athletic profile.

The round-1 weakness across all periods, on the other hand, remains the lingering question mark. There are various possible explanations: first, the 49ers were statistically unlucky (Foster and Lance were both character risks that materialized). Second, the system may overrate top talents with a high athletic profile who ultimately don't have the "football IQ profile" that Shanahan's complex offense demands. Third, the sample is small: nine R1 picks in nine years, three of which were catastrophic.

## Excursus: OTC metrics, roster retention and the definition of draft value

Besides the wAV metric, which relies heavily on career honors and evaluations, it is worth looking at the objective evaluation model of the cap specialists at Over The Cap (OTC). For 2017–2025, OTC's rookie class evaluation uses two primary metrics to systematically measure a front office's success:

- **Metric #1: snap counts and the snap index.** This measures how many snaps a rookie plays in his first four accrued seasons for the team that drafted him (or signed him as a UDFA). The more snaps are covered by cheap rookie contracts, the more cap space remains for established superstars. The most recent classes (2023–2025) are still building their four-year value, but those who get on the field early (like Ji'Ayir Brown or Dominick Puni) are already driving the index up. Here the Niners were even No. 1 in the league up to the Trey Lance draft, then fell back to 25th during the period affected by the Lance trade (2021–2023), but have been back at 5th over the last two years.
- **Metric #2: vested veteran contracts (second contracts) and roster retention.** The supreme discipline of draft evaluation. The vast majority of NFL players never reach a so-called vested veteran contract (a new contract after the four-year rookie period ends). A directly measurable proxy for this quality metric is roster retention: how many of the drafted players are still on an NFL roster after their rookie deal?

### The concrete numbers (2017–2023): 49ers in 2nd place

The data impressively confirms this quality. If you count the players from the 2017 to 2023 draft classes who successfully stayed on an active NFL roster after their rookie contract (whether in San Francisco or elsewhere), the 49ers are among the absolute elite:

| Rank | Team | Active players (drafts '17–'23) |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | Baltimore Ravens | 53 |
| 2 | San Francisco 49ers | 45 |
| 3 | Dallas Cowboys | 43 |

The 49ers shine in this metric, second in the league. Players like Kittle, Warner, Samuel or Greenlaw prove that John Lynch and his team recognize real talent early and retain it for the long term. Only the Ravens (53) are ahead of them, thanks to their immensely high pick volume (compensatory picks).

### Voices from the league: John Lynch and true draft value

Numbers are one thing, the perception of experts another. On The Athletic Football Show, John Lynch's role as GM and the definition of "value" in the draft were recently discussed at length. The experts' statements sum up the 49ers phenomenon perfectly:

> "I think very highly of the 49ers organizationally just in general, like their whole operation is very enviable to me, but clearly they're not infallible… the Trey Lance thing is one of the most horrendous decisions in recent memory. […] It's also kind of impressive that you could screw up that badly and still have a generally favorable reputation, which I think they do and they deserve."
>
> The Athletic Football Show

This quote hits the very core of the criticism of Lynch: the Trey Lance pick was a massive failure. But the front office's work overall is so extremely strong (see OTC metric #2) that the 49ers' reputation in the league remains intact. A single (if expensive) mistake does not define a general manager's entire, otherwise excellent body of work.

And what does real value in drafting actually mean? On the same podcast, Robert Mays discussed how top teams generate "value" in the first place, often simply by accumulating picks (e.g. through the compensatory pick system):

> "Give yourself as many bites at the apple as humanly possible. I always want to be making more draft picks than anybody else… and I'll take my chances that I'm eventually right."
>
> Robert Mays, The Athletic Football Show

This is exactly the most important context for the period after 2021: while other elite teams stayed successful through the sheer volume of picks, especially early ones ("bites at the apple"), the 49ers had to make do with far less high-caliber ammunition because of the expensive trades for Lance and McCaffrey. The fact that they still stand so solidly in the OTC metrics over 2017–2025 proves that John Lynch and his scouting team capitalized above average on the few chances they had left.

**Conclusion on the roster metric:** whether you measure by quality/impact (wAV) or pure longevity (active NFL players), the result is the same. The numbers fundamentally refute the "bad drafter" narrative.

## Conclusion: judge with nuance instead of condemning across the board

Is John Lynch really such a bad drafter? The data's answer is: no, but the picture is more nuanced than a simple yes or no.

**What the numbers clearly show**

- **Top quarter of the league (rank 7/32, 2017–2025).** 77 picks, average wAVOE +1.62, better than 25 other franchises, despite three catastrophic first-round picks including the overpriced Lance trade.
- **Day-3 scouting at the very top of the league.** An R5 average of +9.51 OE over the full period; +16.36 OE in the rebuild phase, unique in the league. Kittle, Purdy, DJ Jones, Hufanga, Greenlaw, Jennings: that's a system, not a lucky streak.
- **The draft is fundamentally hard, for everyone.** Even the league's best drafter (BUF) gets only 24% of its picks to a lasting starter level. Anyone who expects to "win every draft" doesn't understand the business.

**Where criticism is justified**

- **Round 1 as a systematic weakness.** Average wAVOE −6.47 over nine years, negative in all three periods. Solomon Thomas, Reuben Foster and Trey Lance aren't bad-luck cases but evaluation mistakes. Real room for improvement.
- **The competitive window is structurally weak.** Targeted roster optimization instead of BPA, a lack of pick inventory and, in 2022 and 2023, real scouting mistakes (Jackson, Davis-Price, Gray, Latu). League average with Purdy, near the bottom without him.

**Is there hope, and is it justified?**

Yes. 18 of 19 players from the 2024 and 2025 classes are still on the roster. With the 2026 class, Lynch signals that he wants to learn from his mistakes: eight picks, consistent talent scouting, not a single pure roster fill, even if the RB pick in round 3 remains largely incomprehensible, whether because of the position in general, the poor track record or the already full RB room.

**Cycles are normal, even for good GMs:**

Seattle Seahawks (John Schneider): 2017–2021 rank 29 (−2.88 OE), 45% bust rate. Since 2022, rank 5 (+1.18 OE). Same organization, much better results.

Green Bay Packers (Brian Gutekunst): 2017–2021 rank 21 (−1.15 OE). Since 2022, rank 7 (+0.75 OE). No fresh start; the cycle has turned.

Bad phases are part of it. They are not a verdict on a front office's quality.

## The big picture

With the capital available, Lynch and Shanahan built one of the most competitive teams of the last decade: two Super Bowl appearances, an NFC West title, regular playoff presence. A distinction should be made between the build-up phase after Shanahan and Lynch took over (2017–2020) and the all-in phase including the expensive QB trade (2021–2023), whose effects are still felt today. The draft is one part of this story. Some, including the author, also argue that the draft's influence is significantly overestimated because of the media attention it gets. Free agency, trades, cap management and player development are the other parts. There is room for improvement, hope is justified, and panic, as so often in NFL discourse, is hard to reconcile with the data.

Nuance instead of condemnation: that would be a start.
